newsitem.title: FRANCE: Highlights of French government policy statement.
newsitem.headline: Highlights of French government policy statement.

text.p: Following are the highlights of a keynote policy speech given by French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin to parliament on Thursday.
The translation from the French text was done by Reuters. PLEDGES
The commitments made before the French people during the campaign will be honoured.
Nothing is more alien to France than xenophobia and racism. France must define a firm, dignified immigration policy without renouncing its values or compromising its social balance.
We must return to the republican spirit...Let's make a pact: a republican pact, a pact for development and for solidarity. PUBLIC SERVICES
We will end the policy of suppressing jobs in the public services. PUBLIC FINANCES AND MINI-BUDGET

I am asking the economy, finance and industry minister, and secretary of state for the budget to work with the National Assembly and Senate finance committees to present, next week, the first outlines of the government's economic and financial policies.
They will also consult members of parliament in the preparation of the 1998 budget, since the legislative election precluded the organisation of a debate on budget orientations.

The submission of a mini-budget would have called for an extraordinary parliamentary session ending around mid-August. It would have anticipated the results of the audit of public finances, which will not be available before mid-July. This is why I am not presenting a mini-budget now.
The financial measures that the government will undertake will be presented to parliament in the autumn mini-budget.
The amount of legislative work awaiting us will probably call for an early beginning of the parliamentary session, by mid-September. SUPERPHENIX

The power of decision-making must not be taken away from democracy...This requirement is especially clear concerning the setting up of large public infrastructure with important economic, ecological and human consequences.

If the nuclear industry is a major asset for our country, it cannot be outside democratic rules nor pursue projects whose cost is excessive and whose success is uncertain: this is why the fast-breeder (nuclear reactor) known as Superphenix will be dropped. LAYOFFS

Since being elected, I have been confronted with the consequences of the (Renault) Vilvoorde (car plant) conflict. I do not want to see this situation reproduced. Job-cutting plans should be a last resort after the end of genuine negotiations.

I have asked the minister of labour and solidarity to re-examine legislation on layoffs for economic reasons, with the aim of preventing it from leading to insecurity for workers and legal uncertainty for companies.
Based on the report, the government will present draft legislation to parliament...I said it during the campaign. I repeat it today. Jobs are our priority. EMU AND SOLIDARITY

The feebleness of growth is a problem facing the whole of Europe. There must therefore be a common response. In this perspective, we reaffirm our determination to achieve economic and monetary union at the deadline provided for by the (Maastricht) treaty.

But you cannot share a currency without creating economic solidarity. Concerning the independence of a (European) central bank, it does not mean a political vacuum. That was the meaning of the proposals we made (at this week's European Union summit) in Amsterdam.

In a very short time, we have been able to obtain from our partners, on the one hand the approval of a resolution on growth and jobs, which comes in to balance and complete the stability pact, and on the other hand, the holding of an exceptionnal summit meeting on employment.

Such shifts in direction are the result of a difficult negotiation, started in an unfavourable context, since when it came into office the government found a situation which seemed cast in stone. France had given its word on the stability pact.

The pledges I have taken are of course not ending with this first result. We must pursue this path with tenacity. The policy which I intend to follow on European matters, within the scope of my competences, will go towards a strengthening of the (European) union, provided it is above all at the service of the people who make up Europe.
We will march towards a Europe which is more social, a guarantor of progress, peace and independance...In our country, we must bring together the conditions for stronger growth.
To start such a policy, we first need to know the real state of our public finances. We are assessing them for 1997, the results of the audit will be presented to me in July.
The first indications given to me allow me to think that the situation of public finances is serious.

I have already spoken of my committment to the stabilisation of mandatory contributions, which have risen sharply over the last three years. If growth allows, my target is to reduce them in the longer term.

To promote employment and social justice, we must tax income from work less and eliminate the undeserved priviledges that other sorts of income enjoy. We will gradually transfer payroll charges that pay for health insurance onto a widened social levy that applies to all income including investment income.
To sustain growth, we need taxation which does more to favour consumption.
I am asking the economy, finance and industry minister to examine the scope for a reduction in value added tax. HOUSING, FAMILIES, MINIMUM WAGE

An exceptional programme renovating one million housing units will be implemented before the end of this term of office...Personal housing subsidies will be updated and re-valued - they had not been re-valued since 1994.

From September, the allowance for children starting the school year, written in the budget by the previous government, will be raised to 1,600 francs from 420 francs. The state will take its responsibilites to prevent any child from being excluded from school cafeterias for financial reasons...Family allowances will be restricted to households with an income under 25,000 francs (per month).

The government will propose to the National negotiation committee an increase of four percent in the SMIC (minimum wage). Considering a rise in prices of well below one percent, this is the biggest rise in purchasing power for 15 years.
The priority is to create jobs, a lot of jobs. It is the 'raison d'etre' for all government actions.
WORKING HOURS

We must launch a negotiated decrease in working hours designed to favour employment. Reducing working hours without cuts in wages represents both an economic progress - likely to create many jobs - and a social progress.

This is why, in agreement with unions and employers, the shift from a 39-hour to a 35-hour working week will be implemented. It will be the mission of the National Conference on wages, employment and working hours to establish a general framework and debate on all aspects of this process. This conference will open in September.

A parent act bringing the legal working week to 35 hours before the end of the term of office, and limiting excessive use of overtime, and favouring chosen part-time work will be presented at the outcome of the conference.

The state will give its support, notably a financial support, to companies which implement innovative agreements (on jobs) as well as to companies with large workforces, to prevent their competitiveness from being jeopardised.
In this battle for employment, we are lucky enough to have great public services, performing companies active on the international scene.

The economy in France has always relied on a strong public will. We must not break this tradition of ours. One must distinguish public services from the public sector. Public services come under a fundamental view of society, to which we are committed above everything else. They are at the heart of social ties. They guarantee to all citizens an equality of access and treatment, in the provinces or in Paris, in cities or in the country. Some contribute to our energy independence. This is why we refuse to see them turned into objects of profit.
I am acknowledging that the public sector, be it in telecommunications, electronics, aerospace or other sectors, is at stake (in the battle) for ownership.
In the absence of a justification based on the national interest, we are not in favour of the privatisation of this shared heritage that the big state enterprises in competitive industries represent.
Even so, it will be necessary for them to adapt in order to retain our rank among the most developed nations of the world and to get closer to other European partners.
PENSION FUNDS
The measures recently adopted on (private) pension funds, which could do damage to the shared retirement benefit regime, will be called into question. HEALTH

An equal access to health, to learning and to justice must be guaranteed. Universal health insurance will be put in place. Control of health spending is essential. But for the future, we must adapt the current framework. A national health conference - to be held in early 1998 - will allow us to redefine goals and resources to allow all in health care systems to fulfill their mission better.
DEFENCE CONSOLIDATION

Europe is important for our defence. The government hopes to instill a new dynamism in the co-operation that will develop in this area. It is thus urgent to adopt a new and more coherent policy for the defence industries.
Our (defence) enterprises must consolidate, to restore and increase their competitiveness so they can fully participate in future co-operation projects in Europe.
